Result: **主结果（12 次/方法，按设置与种子配对）**：Opus 平均用 53.8 个数据 epoch（省 32.8%，sd 7.3），Δ80=−0.31 pp（95% CI −0.72~+0.09，3 胜 9 负），ΔF=+0.18 pp（p=0.52）；Sonnet 63.8（省 20.3%），Δ80=−0.17 pp，ΔF=+0.15 pp；rule 60.0（省 25.0%），Δ80=−0.19 pp，ΔF=+0.29 pp（p=0.09）；a-priori rule 75.7（省 5.4%），Δ80=+0.02 pp，ΔF=+0.13 pp。Opus 比 Sonnet 多省 12.5 pp（CI 2.8~22.2，p=0.011）且前沿差距相同；Opus 与 rule 无法区分（多省 7.8 pp，p=0.31）。**架构差异**：ResNet-18 上 Opus 最激进（每窗 4.4 个 V），省 38.8% 但低 0.94 pp（前沿差 −0.20 pp），其大部分损失其实来自较短预算（该数据量下配方自身已低 0.74 pp）；ViT-Tiny 上三者均超前沿（Opus/Sonnet +0.62 pp、rule +0.80 pp），但该前沿仍在上升或噪声大。**行为分析（167 次调用、全部通过 dry run）**：Opus 在 12/12 运行中于首个分析点就自发选择快照平均（81 个含 V 的程序中 80 个求平均，1 个沿最近权重变化走一步，均未使用梯度/优化器缓冲/逐层规则），其 301 个被接受虚拟 epoch 中 284 个是平均，权重移动量中位数为数据 epoch 的 73%，验证精度 +2.78 pp，26.2 个节省 epoch 中 23.5 来自"实质性"虚拟 epoch；Sonnet 则多沿 epoch 梯度做小步 SGD（27）、重放动量/Adam 矩（19）、外推（12），其 178 个被接受虚拟 epoch 中 87% 权重移动 <5%（"近似空操作"），16.2 个节省中 12.8 来自此类几乎无效的 epoch；rule 的 75 个窗口中 68 个在第二个 V 槽位重复接受与第一个完全相同的状态（无进展），150 个虚拟 epoch中仅 8 个采用外推。a-priori rule 的 92 次外推尝试有 70 次被拒（中位 −9.4 pp），仅在末窗（epoch 71–80，学习率近零）接受 22 个"近恒等"虚拟 epoch，相对权重变化 4e-4（Opus 为 9e-2）。**开销**：Opus 节省 22.5% GPU 时间（rule 19.6%、Sonnet 12.1%），其中 10.3 pp 被验证前向、BN 重校准、程序调用与梯度记录吃掉；MobileNetV2/CIFAR-100 的计时异常（记录梯度反而更快）若按保守值计价，Opus/Sonnet 的节省降至 20.8%/9.7%。Opus 每次调用平均 29 秒、每运行额外 3.0 分钟，而 80-epoch 配方仅 6.1 分钟 GPU 时间、Opus 只省 1.4 分钟；计入延迟后 Opus 运行比配方长 39%、Sonnet 长 174%；每个节省的数据 epoch 对应 6.8 秒（Opus）延迟，而一个数据 epoch 仅 2.0–5.9 秒。API 成本：Opus 0.68 USD/运行（平均 2.62 请求/次调用）、Sonnet 0.89 USD（5.71 请求），24 次 agent 运行共 18.92 USD。**到目标精度所需数据 epoch**：配方平均 66.4 个，Opus 在 12 次中 8 次以平均 39.1 个达到目标，但与"事后挑选的最优预算"相比优势在 12 次运行分辨率下不可分辨。**方差与稳健性**：同设置同种子的两次 Opus 运行分别用 65 与 73 个数据 epoch；两种模型都不支持采样参数，无法用种子固定决策。

Conclusion: **结论**：GradReason 证明了一件窄而重要的事——在给定一次运行的权重/梯度历史、且提示中不提示任何技术的情况下，LLM（Opus）几乎总能在首次分析时自主发现"最近快照平均"可安全替代数据 epoch，从而以约三分之一的更少数据 epoch 取得与标准配方几乎相同的精度（−0.31 pp，落在噪声内），并位于配方自身的"数据量-精度"前沿之上或持平（+0.18 pp，不可与 0 区分）。但节省的真正来源是这一已知技术（SWA/LAWA）的选择，而非 LLM 的元学习能力本身：同样机制配合先验外推只省 5.4%，加入平均后省 25.0%，与 Opus 无可分辨差异。LLM 的价值在于"在单次运行内发现一个可用更新"（相当于替人类省掉先导实验），一旦该更新已知，固定规则即可零 API 成本、零延迟地复现其效果。

**局限**：① 快照平均并非新方法，其知识已在两个模型的训练截止时间之前，且提示词在主实验前曾含"对噪声主导的梯度求平均"的引导（主实验已移除，但先导实验污染无法完全排除）；② 接受规则只守护单步而不守护累积结果——124 个逐步通过的虚拟 epoch 仍让 ResNet-18 落后 0.94 pp，且允许"近似恒等"更新通过；③ 评测规模小（3 个小架构、2 个 32×32 数据集、每设置 2 个种子、单一供应商、80 epoch 时钟），收益依赖小批量高学习率 SGD 的强噪声这一特定条件；④ 方法并非真正"无数据"——仍需 5,000 张留出图像做前向接受与 BN 重校准；⑤ 沙箱不是安全边界，LLM 供应商会收到摘要统计甚至个别权重值；⑥ 在 CIFAR 规模上墙钟成本高于收益，训练串行等待 LLM 是主要瓶颈。

**开放问题**：需要"正确更新尚未被已知"的场景（标签噪声、类不平衡、其他优化器）来检验真正的发现能力；需要 epoch 成本高于 LLM 延迟的大模型场景；工程方向为让调用与训练并行、接受规则做前瞻式或累积式比较、使用开权重模型以将训练状态留在本地。

Abstract: Standard training recipes make a fixed number of passes over the training data, even when an epoch mostly adds mini-batch noise. We study whether a large language model (LLM) that reads the weight and gradient history of a run can replace some of these epochs with updates that compute no gradient and read no training image. In GradReason, an LLM agent is called every ten epochs. In a restricted sandbox, it analyses recent weight snapshots, epoch-mean gradients, and validation metrics, then submits a Python program that computes new weights and a plan marking each of the next ten epochs as data or virtual. A virtual epoch is kept only if it passes a forward-only check on 5,000 held-out validation images. In 120 runs on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with three architectures, Claude Opus 5.5 used 32.8% fewer data epochs than the 80-epoch recipe at 0.31 percentage points lower test accuracy (95% CI -0.72 to +0.09; 0.94 points on ResNet-18), on the recipe's own frontier of data against accuracy. Unprompted, Opus averaged recent weight snapshots in every run. This choice produced the savings: a fixed rule with the same acceptance check but extrapolations from prior work saved 5.4% of the data epochs, and the same rule with averaging added saved 25.0%. The LLM's contribution is to find a working update within a single run; once found, a fixed rule implements it equally well. An Opus run cost 0.68 USD, but at this scale the agent's latency exceeded the GPU time it saved.

</details>


### [342] [PIA: Agentic Physics-Informed Runtime Anomaly Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11009)
*Ali Mohammadi Ruzbahani,Abbas Yazdinejad,Hadis Karimipour*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: 本文提出 PIA（Physics-Informed Agents）：让大语言模型智能体在部署前充当"水力工程师"，用受限表达式语言编写一小组物理残差（泵特性、罐体质量平衡、站间水头关系、控制器逻辑），并通过一个只含正常运行数据的评估工作台（工具集）反复证伪、迭代，最终部署的检测器是确定性的、可解释的、物理残差形式，运行只需毫秒级且能指出报警对应的部件。在 BATADAL 水分配网络基准上（43 个信号、测试集 7 个攻击），Claude Opus 5.5 版本测试集 F1 达 0.878（最强基线 PCA 为 0.504），召回从 0.349 提升到 0.874，竞赛总分从 0.784 提升到 0.927，且对所有检出的测试攻击都完成了部件级归因；消融表明"用数据检验假设"是关键（去掉工作台最多损失 0.28 F1），而植物描述主要贡献于语义归因（定位准确率 0.714→1.0）。


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: 针对网络物理系统（CPS）的运行时攻击检测存在两条路径但各有缺陷：(1) 从正常数据学习分布的黑盒模型（自编码器、循环预测器）只建模传感器联合分布，无法识别"每个信号单独都落在正常区间内"的隐蔽篡改（重放水位、偏移压力读数），且报警不指明故障位置；(2) 手工推导的物理残差检测器虽能捕捉耦合关系违例，却需要为每个工厂/水厂由专家逐条推导、参数化与调参，工程成本极高。此外，已有"物理信息机器学习/稀疏回归/方程发现"类工作仍假设候选关系项由建模者给定，而 LLM+自动评估器的方法尚未落到轻量、可解释的运行时检测器上。目标是让 LLM 承担"提出物理关系"这一工程工作，同时用正常数据对每条关系做实证检验，从而自动产出与领域专家手写相当、兼具物理残差灵敏度与可解释性的检测器。

Method: **任务形式化**：将 CPS 运行时异常检测表述为"智能体化程序合成"。观测为混合连续传感量与二值执行器状态的多变量流 x_t，每个信号归属物理部件集合 K（罐、泵、阀、节点）；防御方仅有正常数据 N 与工厂的自然语言描述 P，无攻击样本。检测器为受限残差表达式语言中的程序 φ 加参数 θ，设计目标为 max_sens Sens(φ,θ) s.t. FAR(φ,θ)≤α；攻击与灵敏度在设计期不可得，因此必须依赖物理知识去推理"哪种关系会被篡改破坏"。

**残差语言与检测器形式**：每个残差 k 由目标表达式 g_k 和输入表达式 h_k 组成，表达式语言支持算术、比较、逻辑、滞后、差分、滚动均值/求和、条件选择，可表达流量与压力关系、离散化质量平衡、可编程控制器的迟滞逻辑。原始残差 r_k,t = g_k(x≤t) − θ_k^T[h_k(x≤t), 1]，θ_k 由最小二乘在正常数据上拟合，从而吸收水箱截面积、泵增益、摩阻系数等智能体不知道的常数，关系结构来自智能体。每个残差按中位数与 MAD 标准化，|u| 在智能体自选短窗 w_k 上平均，再除以正常数据上端分位数，得到统一尺度（1 表示正常边界）；检测分数 s_t = max_k u_k,t，阈值 τ 取正常数据上分位数。每个残差登记其涉及的物理部件，报警片段按累计 u_k,t 最大的残差归因到相应部件。

**评估工作台（四类工具）**：① 汇总所有信号的正常数据统计；② 将任意表达式与所有信号做相关性分析；③ 在一部分正常数据上拟合并在另一部分上评估，返回解释方差、误报率、评估/拟合尾分位数之比（暴露漂移或过拟合）、以及对合成篡改的检出比例（各相关信号偏移半个标准差，二值执行器取反）；④ 将候选集合装配成完整检测器并报告误报率、引起误报的残差、以及未被任何残差覆盖的信号。智能体在多轮会话中迭代提交 4–24 条残差后结束；系统提示说明残差形式、表达式语言和"正常时应近似恒定"的原则。

**运行时阶段**：提交的残差在模型不再参与的情况下拟合，部署的检测器完全确定性，每步只评估数十个算术表达式，可在监督系统的采样率上在线运行。

**实验设置**：BATADAL 基准 C-Town 水分配网络，43 个信号（7 个罐水位、11 台泵与 1 个阀的流量与状态、12 个节点压力），一年正常数据、Dataset 2（6 个月，7 个攻击）、测试集（3 个月，7 个攻击）；所有检测器与智能体仅使用正常数据，标签取自官方攻击计划；攻击包括修改送至控制器的读数、改变控制阈值、启动泵、降低泵速，多数通过重放或偏移 SCADA 读数隐蔽，持续 24–110 小时。指标为点式 P/R/F1、分数 AP 及竞赛总分 S。基线六个：PCA(T²/Q)、Isolation Forest、密集自编码器、LSTM 前馈器、LSTM-AE、USAD；统一平滑与分位数阈值规则；随机基线 5 个种子；PIA 用 Claude Sonnet 5.5 与 Opus 5.5，每配置 5 次独立会话，每次限 40 轮。

**消融**：blind（描述压缩为一句、信号匿名化）、无工具（保留完整描述但不看数据）两种配置。

Result: **总体性能**：测试集上 PIA(Opus) F1=0.878（最强基线 PCA 0.504），AP 0.899（基线 0.713），精度与 PCA 持平，竞赛分 S=0.927（基线 0.784）；Dataset 2 上 F1 由 0.628 提升至 0.824。Sonnet 版本 F1 为 0.731（测试集）/0.769（Dataset 2），仍显著优于全部基线。增益主要来自召回：测试集召回 0.349→0.874，因为基线能捕捉攻击起始但一旦隐蔽生效即失效，而残差在整个攻击持续期持续触发。

**检测覆盖与归因**：Opus 的 5 次会话中 4 次检出全部 7 个测试攻击、1 次检出 6 个；每次会话中承载报警的残差都涉及被攻击部件（定位正确率 1.0）。对隐蔽攻击 8/9/12/13，所有基线报警覆盖不超过 36%，PIA(Opus) 覆盖 82%–99%；攻击 13 由相邻两站吸入口水头关系承载，攻击 9/12 由罐 T2 相关的阀与泵站水头/水位关系承载；攻击 14 仅在瞬态附近被所有方法（含 PIA）捕获，属共同局限。

**消融结论**：去掉工作台（不接触数据）使 Opus 在测试集损失 0.28 F1、Sonnet 损失 0.22，且 Dataset 2 同向下降；说明"用数据检验假设"是决定性因素——仅凭描述写出的关系过于松散。而仅看匿名信号的 blind 智能体达到 0.858（Opus）/0.842（Sonnet），其记录显示能识别"二值+连续"信号对为泵、通过相关匹配泵与节点，进而写出水头特性与罐体平衡，即从匿名信号中重建了大部分物理结构。植物描述的作用主要是语义层：定位准确率由 0.714 提升到 1.0（部件命名让残差可绑定到具体设备）。

**成本**：Opus 单次会话平均 52 次工具调用、36.4 万输入 + 2.3 万输出 token、194 秒；Sonnet 38 次调用、91 秒。部署检测器约 20 条拟合表达式，拟合 0.13 秒，在纯 CPU 上对三个月测试期打分仅 33 毫秒，运行期不调用模型。

**机制解释**：水网的主导正常变化来自日需求与泵切换，隐蔽篡改（重放水位/适度偏移）仍落在这些主模态内，重建或预测误差极小；而物理残差隔离出正常波动很小的关系（给定流量下的泵扬程、同一吸水管上两压力的一致性），同样的篡改相对该关系方差是巨大的，故残差在攻击时分数可达阈值的 1–2 个数量级。攻击者要隐藏必须伪造所有参与被破坏关系的读数，且因每个部件有多条重叠关系覆盖，一致的伪造需远超被攻击部件的范围。

Conclusion: PIA 证明"智能体化程序合成"可把 LLM 变成 CPS 运行时检测器的设计者：由 LLM 编写物理残差并逐条用正常数据检验，得到既能暴露隐蔽攻击、又能定位到部件、又几乎零运行开销的可解释检测器，且整个设计过程只需数分钟自动化完成，取代了此前"手建物理模型"这一唯一可行方案。其核心洞见是：LLM 的价值不在于闭式地写出物理模型，而在于"关系结构搜索"——决定哪些信号应被耦合、以何种函数形式耦合，并根据数据反馈修正假设；物理描述在此之上提供语义归因层。论文也明确指出局限与未来方向：攻击 14 这类仅瞬态可辨的攻击仍无法覆盖；未评估残差程序在工厂配置、运行工况或传感器可靠性变化后的在线修订（需在保持可解释性与低运行成本的前提下验证新关系）；尚未扩展到让智能体直接查阅工程文档/网络模型，以及超越部件级的操纵类型归因。部署工作流优势（工程师可逐行审计、单一关系可替换而无需重训其余部分、LLM 成本每厂一次）使该方法适合实际水厂运维流程。

Abstract: Runtime anomaly detectors for cyber-physical systems are either learned as black boxes from normal data, which miss stealthy manipulations that keep every signal inside its normal range, or derived by hand from physical models, which requires expert effort for every plant. We introduce physicsinformed agents (PIA), in which a large language model agent writes the detector itself as a set of physical residuals, such as pump characteristics, tank mass balances, and controller logic, and refines every candidate against normal operating data through an evaluation workbench before deployment. The result is a compact, human-readable detector that runs in milliseconds and names the component behind each alarm. On the BATADAL water distribution attack benchmark, PIA with Claude Opus 5.5 reaches an F1 of 0.878 on the test attacks against 0.504 for the strongest of six statistical and deep baselines, keeps detecting attacks concealed by replayed and offset sensor readings, and attributes every detected test attack to the attacked component. Ablations show that testing hypotheses against data is decisive: agents that write residuals from the plant description alone lose up to 0.28 F1, whereas agents that see only anonymized signals recover most of the physical structure.

</details>


### [343] [Unified Factored Representations Resist Catastrophic Forgetting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11020)
*Joel Lehman,Kenneth O. Stanley*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper explores an unexpected connection between the quality of a neural network's (NN's) internal representation and its vulnerability to catastrophic forgetting. The representational forgetting hypothesis is that networks with unified, factored representation (UFR) can resist catastrophic forgetting without any modification to the underlying fine-tuning algorithm or network architecture. The key insight is that catastrophic forgetting may largely result from fractured entangled representation (FER): fine-tuning on only part of the input domain results in disruptive changes for other input patterns, because of how individual features are globally entangled. In contrast, if a gradient update is compatible with how a UFR network factors its representation, such an update may result in coordinated change across the input domain, alleviating catastrophic forgetting. Experiments in two domains provide evidence for this hypothesis: (1) an illustrative 1D regression task, in which UFR networks constructed by hand are compared against networks trained from scratch with SGD, and (2) an image-regression task with NNs previously shown to exhibit UFR. In both settings, UFR networks forget substantially less than their FER counterparts when repeatedly fine-tuned on UFR-compatible variations. Further experiments show that a training loss that distills UFR representations into fresh NNs reduces forgetting; along with several additional controls, these results help isolate representation as the critical factor. Together these results suggest that representational quality is an underappreciated contributor to catastrophic forgetting, and that the encouragement and maintenance of such quality may require attending to what patterns a particular NN is ready to learn.

### [344] [Where Should Models Run? A Collaborative Inference Framework for Embodied Intelligence in 6G](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11023)
*Wanlu Sun,Zhenhui Yuan,Xiang Ji,Yi Han,Qing Li,Gan Zheng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Embodied intelligence systems rely on fast and reliable inference to enable real-time perception, reasoning, and control. Recent advances in large-scale artificial intelligence (AI) models, including Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, have significantly enhanced the capabilities of embodied agents in complex environments. However, deploying these models remains challenging due to the limited computational resources and energy budgets of robotic platforms. A fundamental question is where inference should be executed. Collaborative inference, which partitions models across end devices, edge servers, and the cloud, has emerged as a promising solution. Yet determining the optimal partitioning point remains an open problem, as it depends on wireless network conditions, model structure, and privacy requirements. This article reviews the state of the art in collaborative inference for embodied intelligence and proposes an edge-centric framework in which the edge coordinates model partitioning and execution. Through both simulation and real-world experiments over WiFi and 5G networks, we demonstrate that the optimal partitioning strategy varies with network conditions and model structure. We further identify latency-minimizing partition points for ResNet-101, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and OpenVLA-7B in collaborative inference between NVIDIA Jetson Nano or AGX Xavier devices and an AGX Thor edge server under varying wireless conditions. Finally, we discuss the future directions for collaborative inference in 6G-empowered embodied intelligence systems.

### [345] [Phase-Conditioned Reward Shaping for Token-Efficient LLM Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11024)
*Zhe Chen,Xiaolin Zhou,Xiyang Hu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Extended reasoning can help language models solve complex problems, but long responses often contain both useful computations and redundant checks. Conventional length penalties encourage shorter responses without distinguishing the functions of intermediate steps. We propose Phase-Conditioned Reward Shaping (PCRS), a framework that combines phase identification with training-time reward allocation. We investigate two classification routes: PCRS-H with a hidden-state classifier and PCRS-T with a frozen text classifier. Our main text classifier implementation assigns overlapping reasoning, execution, and revision labels to native chunks, then uses these labels and exact repetition to adjust existing token penalties. We compare the completed configurations on six mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks and examine four reward-weight settings with the text classifier. Compared with a baseline using token-level length penalties, the default text classifier configuration reduces mean response length by 3.13%; sampled Pass@1 is approximately 62.07% for both methods, while oracle Pass@16 rises from 86.08% to 87.67%. These results show how phase-informed penalty allocation can reduce output volume and improve multi-attempt coverage without inference-time classification.

### [346] [Finite-Sample and Communication-Efficient Networked Information Aggregation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11032)
*Mohammadhossein Bateni,Zahra Hadizadeh,MohammadTaghi Hajiaghayi,Mahdi JafariRaviz,Shayan Taherijam*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Building on SODA 2026 work Kearns et al. (2026), we study learning in directed acyclic graphs in which each agent observes only a subset of the input coordinates and may use the predictions of its parents as additional features. In the finite-sample protocol, the message sent along each edge is the agent's prediction vector on a shared sample, so the communication cost is linear in the sample size $m$. In this paper we study this model under communication constraints. First, we revisit the finite-sample analysis of the full-message protocol. We identify a gap in the finite-sample proof of Kearns et al. (2026) and develop a different argument that establishes a finite-sample population-risk guarantee along paths satisfying deterministic $M$-coverage. Second, we introduce a shared-sketch protocol in which each agent sends a $k$-dimensional linear sketch of its prediction vector instead of the full $m$-dimensional message, where $k\ll m$. We analyze this protocol through a reduction to least squares on the compressed sample together with an oblivious subspace embedding argument. The resulting bound separates statistics from communication: the statistical term is still governed by the original sample size $m$, while the additional error due to compression is controlled by the sketch dimension $k$. For Gaussian sketches, we obtain an explicit high-probability population-risk bound, showing that row subsampling is not the only possible communication-statistics tradeoff for networked information aggregation.

### [347] [Target Recoverability under Selective Labels: A Failure Mode in ECG-Based Acute Coronary Syndrome Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11063)
*Alexander Schubert,Anton Håkansson,Ziad Obermeyer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Medical machine learning models often learn from diagnoses observed only in patients clinicians chose to test. The biases of such selective labels are well known, but less understood is what happens when a diagnosis includes cases the model's inputs cannot detect. Because testing decisions draw on information the model does not see, these cases can appear predictable among tested patients, producing relationships that fail, and can even reverse, among the untested. We formalize this mechanism and show in simulations that it worsens as testing becomes more selective or undetectable cases more common, while models trained only on detectable cases remain informative. We empirically study electrocardiogram (ECG)-based prediction of acute coronary syndrome (ACS), which is confirmed only by invasive testing and whose subtypes differ in how clearly they appear on the ECG. Three ECG foundation models fine-tuned on revascularization, our ACS proxy, performed well among catheterized patients (AUROC 0.740-0.770) but worse than chance for 30-day major adverse cardiovascular events among untested patients (AUROC 0.381-0.478). Models trained on ECG-visible subtypes retained discrimination (AUROC 0.680-0.709), whereas a model trained on unstable angina, which can occur without ECG changes, was inversely related to risk (AUROC 0.310). Under selective labels, effective learning therefore requires prediction targets that can be inferred from the model's inputs and evaluation in the intended deployment population, which often extends beyond the patients who were tested.

Abstract: Medical machine learning models often learn from diagnoses observed only in patients clinicians chose to test. The biases of such selective labels are well known, but less understood is what happens when a diagnosis includes cases the model's inputs cannot detect. Because testing decisions draw on information the model does not see, these cases can appear predictable among tested patients, producing relationships that fail, and can even reverse, among the untested. We formalize this mechanism and show in simulations that it worsens as testing becomes more selective or undetectable cases more common, while models trained only on detectable cases remain informative. We empirically study electrocardiogram (ECG)-based prediction of acute coronary syndrome (ACS), which is confirmed only by invasive testing and whose subtypes differ in how clearly they appear on the ECG. Three ECG foundation models fine-tuned on revascularization, our ACS proxy, performed well among catheterized patients (AUROC 0.740-0.770) but worse than chance for 30-day major adverse cardiovascular events among untested patients (AUROC 0.381-0.478). Models trained on ECG-visible subtypes retained discrimination (AUROC 0.680-0.709), whereas a model trained on unstable angina, which can occur without ECG changes, was inversely related to risk (AUROC 0.310). Under selective labels, effective learning therefore requires prediction targets that can be inferred from the model's inputs and evaluation in the intended deployment population, which often extends beyond the patients who were tested.

</details>


### [348] [System Prompts Affect Response Bias More Than Discriminability in LLM Safety](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11074)
*Mohan W. Gupta,Sandy Tanwisuth*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Large language model safety evaluations often focus on a compliance-refusal tradeoff: models should refuse unsafe requests without refusing safe ones. We argue that this misses a broader form of prompt-conditioned task selection, where the same request can elicit different behaviors depending on the system prompt. We investigate this using a controlled evaluation crossing eight safety-task prompt families with three clarity levels across HarmBench, XSTest, and IHEval. Holding benchmark items fixed, we evaluate 13 models and use signal detection theory to distinguish two possibilities: whether models become better at telling safe from unsafe requests (discriminability), or simply more willing to refuse (response criterion). We find substantial differences in discriminability across models, but system prompts primarily shift the willingness to refuse, with smaller and less consistent effects on discriminability. Increasing prompt clarity makes models more willing to refuse without reliably improving their ability to distinguish safe from unsafe requests. Beyond refusal, prompt families also shift responses among six distinct behavioral policies, including clarification and safe help. Together, these findings show that system prompts primarily change how models respond to safety-relevant requests rather than consistently improving their ability to distinguish safe from unsafe ones.

### [349] [Jointly Optimizing Memory, Computing and Offloading for Energy-Efficient DNN Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11106)
*Yunchu Han,Zhaojun Nan,Sheng Zhou,Zhisheng Niu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: In edge intelligence systems, computation offloading and dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) are widely used to improve energy efficiency. However, as applications like deep neural network (DNN) inference evolve in complexity, their demands for memory resources have progressively increased, establishing memory as a critical bottleneck that impacts both latency and energy consumption. In this paper, we propose a joint optimization scheme integrating memory, computing and offloading for energy-efficient DNN inference. We formulate the energy minimization problem under deadline constraints as a mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) problem, where the main challenge arises from the coupling between offloading and resource optimization. To address this issue, we decompose the original problem into two subproblems under a fixed offloading policy. The local subproblem is transformed into an equivalent geometric programming (GP) problem to derive the optimal memory frequency and computing frequency, while the edge subproblem is solved via convex optimization. An efficient coordinate descent (CD) algorithm is further developed to jointly optimize all variables. Simulation results demonstrate that our proposed algorithm achieves near-optimal performance with the gap from the optimal policy being at most 9.3%, and reduces the energy consumption of devices by up to 16.1% compared with benchmarks without memory frequency optimization.

### [350] [DISCOVER: Online Variance-Guided Data Discovery for Budgeted Multimodal GRPO](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11145)
*Peyman Gholami,Shivam Chandhok,Saber Malekmohammadi,Shayan Shams,Robert Xiao,Leonid Sigal*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Recent advances in reinforcement learning have made verifiable rewards a central post-training paradigm for improving multimodal reasoning. However, methods such as GRPO remain data- and compute-inefficient, spending rollout and annotation budget on prompts that provide little learning signal. We propose DISCOVER, an online data-discovery framework for budgeted multimodal GRPO that enables vision-language models to dynamically identify prompts that are most useful for the current policy. DISCOVER first organizes the multimodal sample pool into semantic clusters and queries a small set of density-diverse representative samples to obtain initial reward observations. During training, it estimates the utility of unannotated samples by transferring sparse reward feedback from queried samples. Since sample utility changes as the policy evolves, DISCOVER dynamically updates these estimates with recency-weighted rollout observations. It then selects only high-utility prompts for annotation using a policy-conditioned score that accounts for reward variance and difficulty. Once the discovery budget is exhausted, DISCOVER continues with utility-based replay. Experiments on ViRL39K and VLAA-Thinking with Qwen3-VL-2B show that DISCOVER substantially improves multimodal mathematical reasoning under a strict 10% unique-sample budget, outperforming budget-matched random selection, hard-example sampling, full-pool GRPO under the same training-step budget, and online selection baselines. Ablations further validate the importance of semantic coverage, online reward transfer, and stable discovery cadence, establishing DISCOVER as a practical framework for data-efficient multimodal RL post-training.

### [351] [Not Yet in the Profile: Uncertainty-Aware Dynamic User Profiling by Learning from Future Interactions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11204)
*Jieyong Kim,Neil Shah,Dong Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: On the Web, user profiling builds compact user representations from interaction histories for efficient personalization, and dynamic user profiling updates them as users' behavior and preferences change. However, new user behavior can be ambiguous, and its interpretation differs across users. To address this, we introduce Uncertainty-aware Adaptive Profile Manager (UAPM), which separates the claims in a user profile from interpretations of new behavior that are not yet confirmed, through a Profile, a Buffer, and a Rulebook. UAPM records user-specific interpretation and update rules in the Rulebook, keeps ambiguous evidence in the Buffer outside the Profile as evidence for later decisions, and writes supported general and situational characteristics to the Profile. We train UAPM with Privileged On-Policy Distillation with Dual Specialization (POPD-DS), which learns from recorded future interactions during training without access to them at deployment. Its first stage, Dual Specialization, distills a stronger model into a current-only Student and a future-informed model that becomes the Teacher. In the second stage, privileged on-policy distillation (POPD), only the fixed Teacher receives future interactions and guides the Student's own management decisions alongside task rewards. Experiments on three Web personalization tasks show that UAPM outperforms multiple baselines under the same downstream input budget, improving on the best same-budget baseline by up to 5%.

### [352] [scBIG++: Learning Across Genes and Cells to Predict Single-Cell Perturbation Responses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11217)
*Jiafa Ruan,Zican Qiao,Zongxin Yang,Ruijie Quan,Yi Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Predicting single-cell transcriptional responses to genetic and chemical interventions supports gene-function discovery and regulatory analysis. Existing studies often focus only on highly variable genes, restricting the expression changes available for downstream analysis. Cells exposed to the same intervention can also show heterogeneous expression responses, with coordinated gene programs active to different degrees. We propose scBIG++, a full-gene perturbation prediction framework that models this heterogeneity by connecting expression-adaptive gene modules with population-conditioned generation. To preserve shared gene structure while accommodating cellular variation, Gene-Relation Clustering organizes genes into common windows, within which Dynamic SoftSub learns expression-dependent submodule memberships. This shared organization enables Set-GCAE to exchange information about corresponding gene groups across control cells, placing individual representations in their source-population context. The cell representations initialize a latent flow, while their pooled summary and the perturbation representation condition response generation. Generated states are decoded into expression profiles covering all assayed protein-coding genes retained after preprocessing, supporting comprehensive analysis of perturbation-induced expression changes. Experiments across six genetic and chemical settings spanning 6,539--19,451 genes demonstrate competitive perturbation-effect recovery and full-gene expression reconstruction under unseen targets and combinations, cross-cell-line transfer, and held-out compounds. Our implementation is available at this https URL .

### [353] [SGA-Sparse: Training Native SwiGLU Gates for Activation-Sparse and Low-Bit LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11223)
*Ruokai Yin,Steven Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Activation sparsity can reduce FFN weight traffic during single-user LLM decoding, but active channels must be identified early enough to avoid fetching unused weights. In pretrained SwiGLU models, training-free routing with the native gate performs substantially worse than routing with the up activation at high sparsity. We show that this ordering reverses after sparsity-aware training. Based on this insight, we introduce SGA-Sparse, which converts pretrained SwiGLU LLMs into fixed-budget activation-sparse models by training the existing gate projection directly as a top-k router. SGA-Sparse updates all model parameters end-to-end while preserving the original SwiGLU activation and introducing no auxiliary router parameters. After approximately 30B training tokens, LLaMA models from 1B to 8B achieve uniform per-token 75-85% FFN channel sparsity while remaining within 0.2-2.7 pp of their original dense checkpoints in average zero-shot accuracy. Because post-training quantization degrades sparsity-trained checkpoints, we further study two complementary quantization-aware training (QAT) recipes: continued-QAT largely recovers performance at 4-bit weight quantization, while joint-QAT performs better for the more aggressive sub-4-bit target. To compare activation sparsity with dense low-bit quantization, we translate the sparsity-induced reduction in weight traffic into an equivalent bit-width. Under this unified weight-traffic metric, our 2.5- and 1.5-bit-equivalent models establish a new accuracy-traffic Pareto frontier: the 2.5-bit-equivalent models match dense 3-bit QAT accuracy, while the 1.5-bit-equivalent models approach dense 2-bit models and outperform dense ternary models by 1.3 pp on average. These results establish native-gate training as a practical approach for combining high FFN sparsity with low-bit weights.

### [354] [Do Feature Interactions Break Explainability? Provable Explanations for Any-Order Neural Additive Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11224)
*Idan Refaeli,Yizhak Yisrael Elboher,Guy Katz,Shahaf Bassan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Post-hoc explanation methods for neural networks are often heuristic and lack provable guarantees. A common alternative to such methods that was studied in recent years is to compute a cardinally-minimal subset of input features that is provably sufficient to determine the model's prediction. For general neural networks, however, finding such explanations is computationally intractable. In contrast, recent work showed that this problem becomes more tractable for a particular family of neural networks, namely neural additive models (NAMs), though standard NAMs are highly restrictive because they exclude feature interactions altogether. In this work, we study the computation of provably minimal and sufficient explanations for neural networks with restricted feature interactions, bridging the gap between fully general neural networks and purely additive models. We first prove that even with constant-order interactions, the problem is $\Sigma_2^P$-hard, implying that worst-case exponential complexity is unavoidable. We then identify two provably tractable settings: one based on sparsity in the interaction structure and another based on a stronger interaction-aware notion of sufficiency. Under either of these settings, we develop algorithms that compute provable explanations for neural networks with any-order interactions while retaining much of the computational efficiency of additive models. Empirically, we show that these explanations are significantly smaller and faster to obtain than those produced by standard algorithms, while being derived from models that achieve much higher accuracy than standard NAMs. Overall, our results help expand the class of neural networks that admit efficient provable explanations, while clarifying the fundamental role of feature interactions in shaping their complexity.

### [355] [MCSA: Multi-Cutoff Spectral Aggregation in SO(3) Equivariant GNNs for Interatomic Potentials](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11226)
*Junfu Tan,Mengfan Wu,Yu Zhu,Yu Shi,Yifang Qin,Chang Liu,Bonan Zhu,Ziheng Lu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials (MLIPs) based on Equivariant Graph Neural Networks (EGNNs) have achieved remarkable progress in atomistic modeling. However, accurately representing atomic interactions across different spatial scales remains challenging. In this work, we investigate the radial spectral properties of SO(3)-equivariant message passing and establish that the cutoff radius controls the characteristic spatial-frequency scale of radial interactions. Based on this analysis, we propose Multi-Cutoff Spectral Aggregation (MCSA), a plug-and-play module that aggregates radial kernels with different cutoff radii to enrich multi-scale geometric representations. To achieve efficient implementation, we exploit the compact support of radial kernels to fuse cutoff-dependent radial weights before angular tensor-product operations, avoiding redundant angular computations while preserving rotational equivariance. Extensive experiments across representative EGNN backbones demonstrate consistent improvements in energy, force, and stress prediction, as well as enhanced accuracy in higher-order properties, including phonon dispersion and lattice thermal conductivity. Further evaluations on layered materials with distinct interaction scales demonstrate the effectiveness of physically motivated cutoff selection. Code is available at: this https URL .

### [356] [TLRS-DPO: Token-Level Risk Scoring for Better Direct Preference Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11232)
*Suxin Ji,Hungtao Wan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is a simple and widely used alternative to RLHF for aligning large language models (LLMs), but its sequence-level objective cannot precisely locate or suppress the local patterns that make an otherwise acceptable response unsafe or undesirable. We propose TLRS-DPO (Token-Level Risk Scoring for Better Direct Preference Optimization), which augments DPO with fine-grained token-level control while remaining fully offline and reference-based. TLRS-DPO introduces a token-level robust compensation term that converts the policy-reference log-ratio on rejected responses into localized risk scores, a curriculum-style schedule that gradually increases the strength of this compensation during training, and a risk-adaptive screening mechanism that selectively penalizes only high-risk tokens instead of entire sequences. This design bridges sequence-level preference fitting and token-level behavior control, and can be implemented as a drop-in modification to standard DPO trainers. Empirically, TLRS-DPO improves alignment quality and safety-relevant behavior with minimal impact on helpfulness compared to strong DPO baselines.

### [357] [FRESCO: A Novel Consistency Control for Asynchronous Pipeline Parallel Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11238)
*Dongyeop Lee,Namhoon Lee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Asynchronous pipeline parallelism can accelerate distributed model training, but suffers from instability caused by inconsistent gradient computations. We identify a fundamental source of this inconsistency: error signals are coupled to forward-time features, not just parameter states. This means that parameters may evolve as long as they preserve forward-equivalence. Leveraging this insight, we introduce FRESCO, which frames asynchronous updates as a constrained optimization problem: it finds the minimal update modification that acts trivially on the activation subspace. We demonstrate that FRESCO consistently outperforms representative asynchronous baselines in LLM pre-training, with the gains most pronounced under deep pipelines and high inconsistency levels: at pipeline depth 32, it reaches the same loss as the strongest baseline with 43% fewer iterations and 30% less wall-clock time, while requiring 8~921$\times$ less memory overhead. Moving beyond the current limitations, FRESCO establishes a new foundation for high-utilization pipeline parallel training, providing a scalable path for large-model development on diverse, resource-constrained systems.

### [358] [Primitives and Paths: Predicting What Post-Training Can Do from What the Base Model Already Has](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11260)
*Anqi Qu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Does reinforcement learning teach language models new capabilities, or merely amplify ones acquired during pre-training? The literature offers evidence for both: pass@$k$ studies suggest RL reweights latent behaviours while some controlled composition studies demonstrate gains beyond simple amplification. We argue that this question has no answer independent of the capability state of the base model, and propose a two-dimensional state space for post-trainability. The first axis, \emph{effective full-solution support}, measures whether successful trajectories can be sampled under a feasible exploration budget. The second axis, \emph{atomic primitive coverage}, measures whether the constituent skills of a solution can be executed when the burden of composition is removed. Together, these dimensions motivate three regimes -- amplification, composition-limited, and acquisition-limited -- each predicting a distinct empirical signature and calling for a distinct intervention. We propose a prospective measurement protocol and investigate the framework using synthetic composition tasks across three small language models. We find that primitive mastery alone does not guarantee that RL can learn a composition. Checkpoints that execute every primitive reliably can fail to improve when complete solutions are never sampled during training, whereas modest composition supervision that establishes nonzero support enables substantial RL gains. The framework reframes mid-training as preparation for post-training: its role is to move models into states from which RL can operate effectively.

Abstract: Does reinforcement learning teach language models new capabilities, or merely amplify ones acquired during pre-training? The literature offers evidence for both: pass@$k$ studies suggest RL reweights latent behaviours while some controlled composition studies demonstrate gains beyond simple amplification. We argue that this question has no answer independent of the capability state of the base model, and propose a two-dimensional state space for post-trainability. The first axis, \emph{effective full-solution support}, measures whether successful trajectories can be sampled under a feasible exploration budget. The second axis, \emph{atomic primitive coverage}, measures whether the constituent skills of a solution can be executed when the burden of composition is removed. Together, these dimensions motivate three regimes -- amplification, composition-limited, and acquisition-limited -- each predicting a distinct empirical signature and calling for a distinct intervention. We propose a prospective measurement protocol and investigate the framework using synthetic composition tasks across three small language models. We find that primitive mastery alone does not guarantee that RL can learn a composition. Checkpoints that execute every primitive reliably can fail to improve when complete solutions are never sampled during training, whereas modest composition supervision that establishes nonzero support enables substantial RL gains. The framework reframes mid-training as preparation for post-training: its role is to move models into states from which RL can operate effectively.

</details>


### [359] [Chatter Attack: Resource Consumption Attack for Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11261)
*Yibo Miao,Yichuan Cao,Xiao-Shan Gao,Yinpeng Dong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LLMs are powerful but incur substantial inference cost, which can be exploited by malicious users to induce overly long outputs, increasing latency and operational expense. Prior resource consumption attacks either coerce repetition or suppress the end-of-sequence token by lowering its logit value. However, with autoregressive, sampling-based generation, the search space grows exponentially with length and small deviations or unstable trajectories can derail optimization, limiting attack effectiveness and stability. To address this issue, we introduce Chatter Attack, a novel class of resource consumption attacks that optimize adversarial prompts to induce predefined short target phrases, thereby avoiding search-space explosion while still eliciting long responses. Specifically, Chatter Attack triggers self-doubt using short doubt-inducing phrases as the target, and sustains this state throughout generation via inference attention loss and global entropy loss. To extend to black-box settings, we further propose a novel Bayesian Prompt Optimization (BPO) method, which models the objective function globally by constructing a discrete token kernel, efficiently exploring the entire search space using prior information. Extensive experiments across multiple models and datasets show that our method outperforms baselines, with maximum response length increases to 31.5$\times$, and revealing practical resource-depletion risks for real-world LLM inference services.

### [360] [Beyond Node Attributes: A Controlled Evaluation and Ablation of Local Interaction Statistics for Ethereum Phishing Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11263)
*Thanh Dat Tran,Duy Loi Duong,Duy Luu Hoang,Minh Huy Tran,Vo Minh Thu Le,Nhat Tung Le*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Methods for detecting phishing accounts on Ethereum are usually evaluated as complete pipelines that differ in features, architecture, and training protocol, which makes the contribution of interaction information hard to isolate. This paper evaluates the Unlabeled Feature Extension (UFE), a block of 12 local interaction statistics computed from each account's incoming and outgoing call and transfer edges without reading class labels. UFE is appended to the 14 source features of HEIG-Phish and tested with six model families: Logistic Regression, Random Forest, LightGBM, Graph Attention Network, GraphSAGE, and Meta-IFD. Within each pair of Baseline and Plus variants, the data partition, model configuration, random seed, decision threshold, and sampled neighborhoods are identical; only the input feature block changes. Across 20 predetermined stratified partitions of the same 2,763 labeled externally owned accounts, UFE increased test Macro-F1 by 1.0 to 9.1 percentage points across the six models. Every pair improved on all 20 partitions, all Nadeau-Bengio corrected 95% confidence intervals lie above zero, and the false-positive rate decreased for all six models. An exact-edge Random Forest ablation over 10 predetermined partitions associates most of the gain with the incoming transfer-edge sum attribute; once this feature is present, an incremental contribution of the remaining 11 UFE columns was not established. The results support reporting feature-augmented baselines alongside graph models, but they show stability under re-partitioning of one static, transductive benchmark rather than temporal or cross-dataset generalization.

### [361] [A Unified Framework for License Plate Identification and Character-Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11289)
*Saurabh Kumar,Dewant Katare,Prakriti Jain*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents a unified framework for license plate detection and character recognition on low-power edge hardware. The proposed network uses a shared CSP-Darknet and PANet feature encoder with an anchor-free localization head and a RoIAlign-based sequence-recognition branch. Character decoding is performed directly on aligned feature maps, avoiding image-space plate cropping and a second recognition backbone. The model is trained on an AI-assisted dataset of approximately 37,000 manually verified images covering license plate layouts from all 50 United States. The dataset includes variations in illumination, viewpoint, weather, blur, occlusion, and plate design. The framework is converted to an INT8 TensorRT engine and evaluated on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano with 8 GB memory. The INT8 model shows an mAP50 of 97.8% and a full-sequence accuracy of 90.7%. It records 147 FPS at 6.8 ms end-to-end latency, with 315 MB inference memory and 9.4 W average power consumption. Relative to the YOLOv8s+CRNN baseline, the proposed deployment provides a 7.1x throughput increase and a 77.8% reduction in allocated inference memory

### [362] [PROLA: Principal-Orthogonal Low-rank Adaptation for Predictive Spatiotemporal Weather Downscaling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11318)
*Minseo Yoon,Minseong Bae,Sojin Lee,Hyunwoo J. Kim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: High-resolution weather prediction is important for resolving local atmospheric patterns missed by coarse global forecasts. Large pretrained weather backbones have improved global forecasting, but adapting them to produce future high-resolution fields from recent coarse states remains challenging and costly. We formulate this setting as Predictive Spatiotemporal Weather Downscaling (PSWD), a task that jointly refines spatial and temporal resolution while predicting future high-resolution trajectories. To this end, we propose a framework that decomposes prediction into spatial and temporal stages using a shared pretrained backbone, fixed numerical scaffolds, and lightweight residual heads. For backbone adaptation, we introduce PROLA (PRincipal-Orthogonal Low-rank Adaptation), which allocates a fixed low-rank budget between pretrained weights' principal directions and their orthogonal complement. PROLA further rescales rank-1 optimizer updates using gradient signals, improving adaptation without increasing trainable rank. Experiments in the PSWD setting show that PROLA outperforms representative low-rank adaptation baselines. Further experiments across diverse datasets and tasks support the broader applicability of PROLA, showing that its benefits extend beyond the primary weather downscaling setting.

### [363] [Where Should a Gate Look? Input vs. State Gating in Diagonal State Space Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11336)
*Riccardo Zattra,Giacomo Baggio,Leonardo De Marchi,Augusto Ferrante,Francesco Ticozzi,Marco Del Prà,Antonio Orvieto*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Modern state-space models owe much of their computational efficiency to their linear, often diagonal, dynamics. Classical recurrent neural networks instead allow nonlinear state-to-state interactions, which can be beneficial when memory updates need to depend on the past context. In this paper, we ask whether state feedback through a simple gate regulating memory updates can enhance the expressivity of diagonal state-space models. To investigate this question, we compare gates that depend on the current input, the recurrent state, or both. We establish a strict expressivity separation: for scalar models, state gating solves induction-head tasks for arbitrary vocabulary size and sequence length, whereas input gating fails on a finite instance under standard stability assumptions on the state transition matrix. Experiments show that state gating retains its advantage on induction-head tasks in higher-dimensional models, whereas input gating performs better on selective copying tasks. Together, our results show that even a simple, diagonal form of state-feedback gating can unlock capabilities unavailable to input-controlled models, while input and state gating offer complementary strengths and achieve the strongest overall performance when combined.

### [364] [Agent Self-Improvement with Frozen Weights: The Added Value and Limits of Failure Traces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11342)
*Arkid Mitra*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: We evaluate whether an AI agent's harness, the notes around its model, can learn from the agent's failure traces beyond a matched search that never sees them. It can, but less than it looks. We tested an open 9-billion-parameter model with fixed weights; a larger teacher model wrote its notes. On generated customer-service decisions, where both note writers were told the target rules, notes based on the agent's mistakes improved accuracy by 4.0 percentage points over notes from the same process with the mistakes withheld. That process alone, trying and keeping better-scoring notes, reached about 60% of the total improvement. In full customer-service conversations the same notes showed no demonstrated improvement. Separately, a strict screen of single lessons admitted two customer-service lessons, still awaiting tests on new data, and one tool-use lesson, written without seeing the agent's mistakes, which showed no demonstrated gain on new tool-use tasks. A neutral note with no procedure scored higher than the learned lessons (exploratory). A blind audit judged 146 of 240 tool-use test items defective.

### [365] [D3Tree: Learning to Prune Block-Diffusion Draft Trees for Efficient Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11371)
*Hong Nie,Zhangchi Gao,Jun Yu,Bo Wang,Jianqing Sun,Shengping Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Block-diffusion drafters propose a whole block of tokens in one forward pass, and draft trees built from their position-wise marginals increase the expected accepted length of speculative decoding. Every tree node occupies a query row in target verification, so under concurrent serving low-yield branches compete with other requests for verification capacity. Existing tree methods select verified nodes by draft probability under a fixed or cost-selected per-request budget, and thus always retain a prefix of the drafter's ranking. We present D3Tree, which learns which nodes of a block-diffusion draft tree are worth verifying. A tree-size head with 2H+2 parameters predicts each candidate's conditional survival from the draft state, the candidate embedding, and its draft log-probability. Thresholding the product of these scores along parent chains yields an ancestor-closed subtree whose size adapts to each request and decoding round. The head is trained on a frozen drafter with conditional labels on the full candidate tree; an optional joint mode also steers the drafter toward the retained reference path. At serving time, D3Tree verifies whole trees under light load and, under heavy load, allocates one batch-wide node budget by predicted survival, sized to the target's matrix-multiplication tiles. Retained trees share one ancestor-masked target pass, while construction, pruning, and scheduling run on the GPU and overlap with the host. Across six vision-language verifiers and 17 text and multimodal benchmarks, D3Tree is fastest in 70 of 72 load settings, with 3.2-4.0x speedup over autoregressive decoding for one request and 1.3-1.8x at 64 concurrent requests, where fixed-budget trees fall below autoregressive speed. Under a time-varying arrival trace, it has the lowest mean end-to-end latency in every arrival phase.

### [366] [LLM-based Multi-Criteria Deep Reinforcement Learning for Dynamic Efficient 5G UPF Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11372)
*Abdelrahman Soliman,Ahmed Refaey Hussein,Lei Lei*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: User plane function (UPF) selection in 5G networks is an active area of research, with various limited approaches proposed to enhance network efficiency and manage resources effectively. In this paper, we address this gap in the related literature by proposing a Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) UPF selection method that utilizes a dynamic, multi-objective reward function and validating it on a real-world 5G emulation platform. The proposed method is based on the large language models' (LLMs) translation of network operator intents and the network data analytics function (NWDAF) abnormality alerts. The experimental results validated in the real-world experimental setup demonstrate that our dynamic DRL solution achieves an effective balance between latency, power consumption, and traffic distribution, outperforming the heuristic baselines and fixed DRL by 16.89%. These findings highlight the real-world applicability of our approach for dynamic, intent-driven UPF selection.

### [367] [The comparison of density estimation for transfer learning in Banach, Hilbert, Euclidean spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11382)
*Maryam Alsadat Kazemian,Azam Bastanfard*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Domain adaptation or DA methods are indispensable when target labels or computational resources are scarce, yet the domain kernel density and subspace alignment approaches completely assume a Hilbertian geometry. They measure distributional discrepancy with symmetric L2 divergences over Euclidean feature spaces or reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS). This preprint summarizes the manuscript Non-Hilbertian Domain Adaptation. Total Variation Alignment via L1 Density Regularization on Feature Manifolds, which proposes Banach Manifold Transfer Learning or BMTL. BMTL makes two coupled design decisions. The first one is that features are embedded on a geodesic manifold rather than treated as points of a flat Euclidean space, and the second one is that the density matching regularizer is formulated in an L1 Banach norm, whose minimization is equivalent, by Scheffe's theorem, to contracting the Total Variation or TV distance between domain densities, a bounded metric that weights all regions of the sample space uniformly. The L2 formulation, by contrast, squares deviations and therefore amplifies errors in the tails, over emphasizing density outliers that do not reflect meaningful distributional shift. Experiments on MNIST-USPS, COIL20, and Office+Caltech10 show consistent gains; the L1 variant beats an otherwise identical L2 ablation on every task, for example 92.44% vs. 89.80% on USPS->MNIST and surpasses the strongest baseline DMDA by +3.68% on average over twelve Office+Caltech transfers. This document situates the contribution with an explicit comparison of Euclidean, Hilbert, and Banach geometries.

### [368] [Learning to Rank Propagators in Constraint Programming](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11447)
*Matija Lojović,Mladen Nikolić*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The order in which propagators are executed can substantially affect the performance of constraint programming solvers, yet propagator priorities are typically determined by fixed, manually designed heuristics. In this work, we explore learning instance-dependent propagator priorities from static problem features. We formulate the task as a learning-to-rank problem, addressing the challenge that the quality of a priority assignment can be measured through solver runtime, while the desired priorities of individual propagators are not directly observable. A self-attention-based model jointly scores the propagators present in an instance and is trained using pairwise preferences derived from solver runtimes measured under randomized propagator priority assignments, with a Plackett-Luce-based ranking objective. Predicted rankings are mapped to the discrete priority levels of the Choco solver before search begins, without modifying its propagation or search procedures. We evaluate the approach on XCSP3 instances and demonstrate that propagator ordering can have a substantial impact on solving time. On a test set of 698 instances, picked out as most difficult by problem class, the learned priorities increase the number of solved instances from 634 to 654, reduce median solver runtime by 27.93%, and reduce aggregate penalized runtime (PAR1) by 12.65% compared with Choco's default priorities. We further observe that improvements vary across problem classes and show that a simple policy selecting between learned and default priorities further increases the number of solved instances. These results demonstrate the potential of learning instance-dependent propagator priorities to improve constraint programming performance, particularly on difficult instances.

### [369] [How Much Training-Inference Mismatch Can On-Policy Distillation Tolerate?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11450)
*Cong Yu,Ziting Wang,Songlin Jiang,Sitong Zhang,Chengliang Chai,Youhe Jiang,Eiko Yoneki,Tuo Shi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student language model on its own responses, guided by a fixed teacher. Generating these responses is expensive, so systems use quantized inference and asynchronous rollouts to reduce the cost. Both, however, introduce training-inference mismatch between the rollout engine and the model being trained. Such mismatch can destabilize reinforcement learning (RL), but its effects on OPD remain unclear. This paper investigates how much mismatch OPD tolerates, where its effects arise, and how training systems can use this tolerance. Measuring all mismatch sources on one scale, we examine quantization across three student-teacher pairs, with additional tests of weight staleness and injected noise on one pair. OPD tolerates substantial mismatch without meaningful loss of training quality but degrades at higher levels, revealing an empirical mismatch budget. Both the quality cost of mismatch and the mismatch introduced by quantization depend on the model, with some layers particularly sensitive to reduced precision. In controlled comparisons, OPD remains stable under rollout configurations that destabilize RL methods. Under weight noise, mismatch also shifts the prefixes reached during generation, introducing errors that per-token corrections cannot address. To put these findings into practice, we introduce a lightweight admission check that screens rollout configurations against a calibrated budget without requiring a full training run for each candidate. Model-specific FP8 recipes preserve training quality while providing capacity for at least $1.93\times$ as many KV-cache tokens as BF16. Combining FP8 with asynchronous rollouts reaches the same training quality $1.62\times$ sooner than synchronous BF16 training. Code is available at this https URL

Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student language model on its own responses, guided by a fixed teacher. Generating these responses is expensive, so systems use quantized inference and asynchronous rollouts to reduce the cost. Both, however, introduce training-inference mismatch between the rollout engine and the model being trained. Such mismatch can destabilize reinforcement learning (RL), but its effects on OPD remain unclear. This paper investigates how much mismatch OPD tolerates, where its effects arise, and how training systems can use this tolerance. Measuring all mismatch sources on one scale, we examine quantization across three student-teacher pairs, with additional tests of weight staleness and injected noise on one pair. OPD tolerates substantial mismatch without meaningful loss of training quality but degrades at higher levels, revealing an empirical mismatch budget. Both the quality cost of mismatch and the mismatch introduced by quantization depend on the model, with some layers particularly sensitive to reduced precision. In controlled comparisons, OPD remains stable under rollout configurations that destabilize RL methods. Under weight noise, mismatch also shifts the prefixes reached during generation, introducing errors that per-token corrections cannot address. To put these findings into practice, we introduce a lightweight admission check that screens rollout configurations against a calibrated budget without requiring a full training run for each candidate. Model-specific FP8 recipes preserve training quality while providing capacity for at least $1.93\times$ as many KV-cache tokens as BF16. Combining FP8 with asynchronous rollouts reaches the same training quality $1.62\times$ sooner than synchronous BF16 training. Code is available at this https URL

### [370] [MOMENT-DP: Momentum Aware Evaluation of Correlated Noise for Differentially Private Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11457)
*Sunny Gupta,Raja Viswanadha*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Temporally correlated noise can substantially improve the utility of differentially private optimization, yet candidate mechanisms are commonly designed or evaluated using only partial information about the optimization process, such as workload structure, learning-rate schedules, or local curvature. We study whether persistent optimizer state provides additional information that can change the relative utility of privacy-valid correlated-noise mechanisms. We introduce MOMENT-DP, an optimizer-state-aware framework that models how temporally correlated privacy noise propagates through momentum-based optimization. For locally quadratic objectives, MOMENT-DP expresses privacy-induced final loss through an optimizer transfer operator that jointly captures curvature, learning-rate scheduling, momentum, and temporal noise covariance. NoiseCurve's curvature-aware quadratic criterion is recovered exactly as the zero-momentum, constant-learning-rate special case. Changing only momentum while holding curvature, schedule, privacy calibration, and candidate mechanisms fixed induces genuine mechanism-ranking reversals. The effect persists outside exact quadratic dynamics in per-example-clipped private logistic regression, while remaining unresolved in the neural regime we study. These results establish optimizer state as an under-modeled, decision-relevant axis in evaluating temporally correlated privacy noise.

### [371] [JoMoHa: Joint Model--Harness Optimization with Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11499)
*Xudong Wu,Guangchen Lan,Mingqi Yuan,Jiayu Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The performance of language agents depends jointly on model weights and the harness. Optimizing either alone can be constrained by the other component, limiting overall performance gains. Our analysis of naive alternating training reveals progressive incompatibility between the model and harness, which increasingly interferes with task execution and may also undermine model training, leading to performance degradation. To coordinate the evolution of models and harnesses, we introduce JoMoHa, to our knowledge the first framework to jointly train an executable harness generation policy and a task execution policy through reinforcement learning. JoMoHa outperforms the evaluated weight-only and harness-only baselines and achieves the highest success rates among the evaluated methods on ALFWorld, WebShop, and DBBench, averaging 70.3% and reaching 97.0% on ALFWorld. By learning both task execution and runtime improvement from its own generated trajectories, JoMoHa performs recursive self-improvement (RSI).

### [372] [Data-informed Adaptation of Foundation Models for Causal Effect Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11504)
*Chunwei Ma,Russell D Wolfinger*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Due to the fundamental problem of causal inference -- the impossibility of observing counterfactual outcomes -- there is always a gap between the training goal (outcome, propensity) and the inference target (CATE, ATE). Traditional causal effect estimation revolves around setting assumptions, selecting identification strategies, and choosing causal estimators, while more recently, Causal Foundation Models (CFMs), built on Prior-Data-Fitted Networks (PFNs), ease this process by pretraining on massive synthetic prior datasets. Despite their success, such amortization makes causal inference less transparent, obscuring which assumptions the model implicitly relies on for a given dataset. The high diversity of real-world data-generating processes (DGPs) and Structural Causal Models (SCMs) makes it hard to know, a priori, which causal inference strategy is compatible with a given dataset. In this work, we focus on this compatibility between an observational dataset and method-specific assumptions, and find that geometric characteristics of data embeddings -- specifically, the variogram -- provide a useful signal of whether a given causal estimation strategy is appropriate. We develop MoE-Learner, a mixture-of-causal-experts framework that embeds a dataset under multiple assumption-specific views and uses the variogram as a counterfactual-free router to assess each expert's validity. Rather than eliminating causal assumptions, this shifts their validation from a fixed, a priori choice to a criterion that can be checked directly from data geometry. MoE-Learner achieves the best average rank on benchmark datasets (IHDP, ACIC, Lalonde). Being orthogonal to (causal) foundation models, our method builds a bridge from data characteristics to causal estimation strategy rather than proposing another CFM.

### [373] [Detecting Common Golfing Faults Using AI and Video-Derived Biomechanical Features](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11515)
*Oliver Martin,Jeff Clark,Nawid Keshtmand*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Understanding how an athlete moves can improve both technique and safety, yet outside the laboratory technique is still assessed by eye. We present a pipeline that detects named golf swing faults from ordinary video, without markers or calibration. Instead of learning end to end, it tracks body pose and the clubhead in a body-centered frame, and classifies the biomechanical quantities a coach would measure, such as the height of the clubhead above the swing plane, with shallow boosted trees. We demonstrate the approach on two common faults, coming over-the-top (OTT) and early-extension (EE). On 160 swings and 143 swings from public sources it detects OTT and EE with a cross-validated ROC-AUC of 0.975 and 0.911 respectively. Because every feature is a biomechanical quantity a coach already uses, measured at a known phase of the downswing, each decision can be traced to the signals and the moments of the swing that drove it. The signals the model relies on most are the same ones a coach checks when diagnosing these faults. The pipeline processes phone video on a consumer laptop in seconds, so it could feasibly be developed into an app for golfers of all abilities and extended to other sports in which technique is judged against a biomechanical reference.

### [374] [Hydra: Towards Transferable Multi-Task Learning on Temporal Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11520)
*Kiarash Shamsi,Farimah Poursafaei,Tran Gia Bao Ngo,Reihaneh Rabbany,Baris Coskunuzer,Guillaume Rabusseau,Michael M. Bronstein,Shenyang Huang,Cuneyt Gurcan Akcora*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Real-world evolving networks are naturally modeled as temporal graphs (TGs), where capturing temporal dynamics is essential for predicting future graph properties that support downstream decision-making. Existing temporal graph methods have been developed primarily for single-task prediction, and little is known about their generalization across tasks or transfer to unseen networks. This leaves the challenge of multi-task graph property prediction in TGs largely open. We address this challenge by introducing Hydra, a novel architecture that integrates local connectivity features from temporal GNNs with a spectral learning module that captures global connectivity patterns. This design enables joint learning of local and global information under a multi-task objective. In multi-task classification, Hydra achieves an 8.9% relative gain in AUC over the strongest competitor. In multi-task regression, Hydra achieves competitive results in all three tasks, while obtaining the best results in two tasks with a 8.2% relative gain in MAE compared to the strongest baseline. Moreover, Hydra delivers these gains with a 22% reduction in training time compared to temporal transfer models. These results provide the first systematic evidence that multi-task transferable learning on temporal graphs is effective. By delivering consistent top-ranked performance, Hydra highlights multi-task training on temporal graphs as a promising direction toward adaptable foundation models for temporal graphs.

### [375] [Boundary Mass in Feature Space as a Label-Budget Diagnostic for Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11525)
*Siming Zhang,Zhehui Shen,Shijie Chen,Yansen Yu,Hang Yu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Low-label transfer is often decided by a practical question: after a representation looks useful, how many labels are still needed to learn the downstream boundary? Transferability and probe-quality scores characterize global alignment, likelihood, margins, and calibration. Boundary-near target mass complements these diagnostics by measuring the ambiguous regions where scarce labels are most costly. We propose effective boundary complexity, a label-budget diagnostic for frozen representations and linear probes. It measures mass in a thin strip around the learned boundary and normalizes it by class balance, so dense ambiguous regions and predicted-class imbalance are both counted. We prove that, under a smooth representation map, density change and tangential surface change cancel at first order, leaving boundary-normal stretch or compression as the governing factor. This yields a cached-feature estimator that fits a probe on one split and counts independent held-out features near its boundary. Experiments support the diagnostic at three levels. Controlled transformations match the predicted law across 74 maps with 0.38% median relative error. On real frozen features, normal-direction changes move both measured boundary mass and label demand, while tangent controls preserve the first-order coefficient. A differentiable surrogate reduces measured complexity by 16-36% at matched top-1 utility. Finally, CIFAR-100 and Tiny-ImageNet experiments support boundary mass as a second-stage diagnostic for near-tied representations. Five-way experiments show strong OvR-interface backbone-ranking agreement (Spearman 0.872), while acquisition experiments show high correlations between initial boundary mass and realized label budgets across three sampling policies (0.779-0.830). Code is available at this https URL .

### [376] [Probing Transformer Representations Layer by Layer, Module by Module](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11531)
*Ambroise Odonnat,Theo Gnassounou,Laetitia Chapel,Romain Tavenard,Ievgen Redko*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Which representation should be probed in a transformer-based foundation model? Recent work shows that the standard practice of probing the final layer is often suboptimal, as intermediate layers can provide better features. Yet, representations are still largely studied along depth alone, treating each transformer block as an atomic unit. In this work, we analyze transformer representations layer by layer, module by module. Through more than 144,000 linear probing evaluations of vision foundation models (VFMs) and large language models (LLMs), we show that layer and module choices should be considered jointly: the best layer-module pair yields substantially larger gains over the final-layer residual stream than the best layer with the residual stream fixed. Moreover, module performance can vary substantially across layers, showing that useful representations cannot be characterized by depth alone. Building on these findings, we evaluate simple fixed probing strategies: the final-layer feedforward activation (Act@100) for vision and the second normalization layer at 60% depth (LN2@60) for language. These strategies improve over the probing baseline in a majority of evaluations and recover, on average, 42% and 86% of the gains from probing the best layer-module pair for vision and language, respectively. For VFMs, these gains increase with the transfer difficulty between pretraining and downstream data.

### [377] [Direct GPU Energy Measurements of Batch-Level Sharing in Mixture-of-Experts and Recurrent Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11696)
*Rafael Pina,Varuna De Silva*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Energy claims for efficient neural networks are often inferred from operation counts. We report direct GPU energy measurements on two workloads that batch very differently, recurrent policies in GPU-vectorised multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) and mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models, and ask one question of both: can the rows of a batch be made to share computation, across the batch and over time, at a measured saving? On recurrent policies the answer so far is no. Shared activity patterns exist but rarely last one step, masking a frozen policy fails, and trained-in masks succeed only because a fixed mask is equivalent to a narrow GRU, at 11x the energy of a small dense policy in our implementation. Test-time steering adds nothing beyond re-picking on either workload. On MoE models the answer is yes, and granularity decides how much: on Qwen3-30B-A3B, batch-aware routing reads 25-31% fewer expert weights within KL 0.05, with benchmark changes within noise at 500 items, and uses 12-18% less energy per token on a fused forward. We also introduce persistence-aware OEA, a one-parameter rule that keeps the batch-aware cut with about 40% fewer new experts per step than native routing at batch 32-64, though its energy has not yet been measured. These are pilot measurements on one GPU type, and we state their limits.

### [378] [Scalable Counterfactual Explanations for Time Series via Policy Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11704)
*Peiyu Li,Pouya Hosseinzadeh,Soukaina Filali Boubrahimi,Shah Muhammad Hamdi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Generating counterfactual (CF) explanations for time series is challenging due to complex temporal dependencies and the computational inefficiency of traditional instance-specific optimization. We propose a policy learning framework for counterfactual explanation in time series, trained as a one-step contextual-bandit policy-learning problem. By training an actor-critic agent in the latent space of a pre-trained autoencoder, our method learns a transferable policy that captures global structural regularities. Unlike existing methods that rely on iterative optimization for each new input, the learned policy enables direct generation of valid and plausible counterfactuals through a single forward pass, avoiding per-instance optimization at inference time. Experiments on 13 UCR benchmark datasets show that our framework achieves high validity and strong plausibility across multiple anomaly detection metrics. Overall, by decoupling counterfactual generation from per-instance optimization, the proposed method provides an efficient and scalable alternative to existing approaches for time series counterfactual explanations.

### [379] [Spectral Rank and Step-Direction Dynamics in Language-Model Post-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11752)
*Khurram Khalil,Khaza Anuarul Hoque*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Language-model post-training modifies weights through cumulative updates and successive displacements, yet existing studies report seemingly conflicting spectral properties: nearly full-rank updates and low stable-rank changes. We show these observations are compatible and characterize update directions during training. For singular values following $\sigma_i \propto i^{-\alpha}$ with $0 < \alpha \leq 1/2$, we prove that stable rank becomes negligible relative to fixed-energy rank as dimension increases. Full singular value decompositions of selected OLMo-2-7B updates confirm this separation: three proximal policy optimization (PPO) attention updates have stable ranks of 9.6-18.3 but require 532-1,222 singular components to capture 80% of their energy. We next compute consecutive checkpoint-displacement cosines from full-model inner products. Across nine publicly released reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) stages, all 131 adjacent pairs have negative cosines on their native checkpoint grids, including PPO and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) trajectories. Supervised fine-tuning comparisons across four model families show configuration-dependent alignment, including negative late-training cosines for Mistral and FP32 Llama. Finally, a controlled OLMo-2-1B study with three paired seeds and a 2,048-token response cap compares group-relative advantages against a learned critic with generalized advantage estimation (GAE). At matched 60-rollout windows, late-training mean cosines are +0.259 and +0.012, respectively; the paired critic-minus-group difference is -0.247 (seed-level 95% interval [-0.358, -0.137]). These findings distinguish spectral concentration, energy coverage, and trajectory direction, and demonstrate that the advantage system influences directional alignment under matched training conditions.

At matched 60-rollout windows, late-training mean cosines are +0.259 and +0.012, respectively; the paired critic-minus-group difference is -0.247 (seed-level 95% interval [-0.358, -0.137]). These findings distinguish spectral concentration, energy coverage, and trajectory direction, and demonstrate that the advantage system influences directional alignment under matched training conditions.

</details>


### [380] [Late but Valuable: Why Deadlines Change the Measured Value of LLM Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11910)
*Sina Barazandeh,Benjamin E. Lundell,Jose Lugo-Martinez*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly plan and run experiments in automated laboratories. These experiments keep running while the model reasons and run on schedules with hard deadlines. If an LLM-generated answer arrives late, the system executes a safe fallback action instead, such as rejecting a sample. This creates a systems problem that standard serving metrics do not capture. An answer that matches the fallback adds no value, and answers that differ from the fallback may require more reasoning time. Reporting answer quality and latency separately can therefore overstate the value of reasoning. We test this on synthetic sample decisions, where the best choice is known exactly and a runtime enforces the deadline. We compare one LLM's fast mode, which answers directly, with its thinking mode, which reasons first. In a prespecified replay of 1,200 new decisions, thinking answers that missed a deadline were worth about five times as much as on-time ones. Multiplying the on-time rate by the mean answer value predicted about twice the value that thinking delivered. This prediction overstated thinking's advantage over fast mode by 0.0241 per decision, and by 0.0191 in a repeat on 300 new decisions. Both 95% confidence intervals excluded zero. In a single-GPU Qwen3-8B experiment using simultaneous request bursts, raising the number of requests from 8 to 56 reduced the share of thinking answers that met a 45 s deadline from 79.2% to 1.4%, although total output tripled. Evaluations of LLM agents for laboratories should therefore measure each answer's value and arrival time together and score the action that actually runs.
